segments.text: The Zwigots

"Receive him, for he is neither stranger nor guest. He comes as water rains on a river from which it first came. Let him return. Let nothing of him be called unclean. Consume him slowly, savor every bite. Until one becomes all and all becomes none."
Zwigoti prayer for the departed
Due Disclosure

I've made arrangements for my burial, and a Zwigot will not be handling it. I want that said before I write anything else about them, because the rest of this chapter is going to sound more generous than I feel, and I'd rather not be mistaken for a sympathiser.
The largest religious movement on the continent, present in most cities, uncontested everywhere except Lastrago, which I'll get to later.
It would seem that, gods or not, people have to believe in something, and on a continent with this much rot, it only makes sense that somebody would build a religion around it.
Prophet Beltzu did, and fourteen centuries later his monks handle the dead in villages that couldn't name a single line from his book. How disappointing. How practical.
More Cults

Beltzu was a Mazuhren priest, ordained in the year three hundred and forty-two, some fourteen fifty-eight years ago. And like the other priests, he was a Car-Rex, taken from his family in Naktzu to be strapped to a spire in Azwighen. Before that it's the usual ladder: years of tutelage underground tasting water out of stone pools.

And then work. He was rather successful for about a decade or so. Not in an extraordinary kind of way, but well enough to make a name for himself. However, in three hundred and fifty-one he read an entire season wrong.

Three readings one after another, resulting in a documented total of one hundred and sixty-nine people missing or dead. He was offered the spire a second time, and chose exile instead. He then marched west onto Trefgann, and that's where the temple's account of him ends.

What remains from his later endeavors survived through the Tzikhari. A few hundred sayings, most of them shorter than this sentence, collected by people who'd heard them secondhand and written down well after he was dead. No biography in it.

No argument either, which irritates me to no end. You've already bothered to write it all down, might as well take the extra step and leave a paragraph where he explains his own words. Instead we're left with these maxims, followed by fourteen centuries of monks arguing.
Novices memorize the whole collection while they're young, and spend the rest of their life disagreeing about it with whoever sits across the table. An obvious influence from the Mazuhren.
Priests were publicly disputing forecasts long before Beltzu was born, and we can safely assume the habit travelled west alongside him.
Words And Their Meanings

Fittingly, as the prophet's original intentions eroded, so did the name. Zwigot, or Tzigot in the oldest of sources. Then Zhigot by the time Remosan clerks had to file it, and lastly: our very own Zwigot, which is a word in no language anyone has been able to point me at.
Experts in ancient Lastragan claim the original meant something close to "not fearful," but I'm afraid I can't confirm that with any confidence.

The Tzikhari has gone through many translations, which eroded the enigmatic original even more. I'll give you an example. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot", commonly translated: "eat what is put in front of you". But this is merely one interpretation. Komak also means sits. Stays. Remains.

You see, several ways to translate, and then several more to interpret each translation. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot". Four words, and they can't even agree whether it's about food. One reads: the thing is there, you eat it, and the eating is the whole of the acceptance.
Another takes it nearer to remains, as in leftovers, as in what the world has already finished with, and that's the reading that ends with a monk face down in mud and human flesh.

The third holds that the sentence is about food and nothing else, and is popular among parents who wish their kids would eat more turnip. Underneath all three sits the same core claim. There is one substance. Not gods, not laws. One substance, and everything is it.

To the Zwigot mind, the Sundering didn't split the world, and the world is not, in fact, being broken apart. Because one substance can't be broken down into anything but the same substance. A rift is the world doing what the world does: recycling.

So is rot, and so is the child whose shadow walks off on its own. The only thing that has actually happened in eighteen centuries is that people insisted on struggling against the obvious, clinging to a world that only wants to be remade.

Which brings us back to Lastrago, since I said I would. The Mazuhren looked at the same sky and built an apparatus for getting out from under it. A priesthood whose entire function is telling you when it's time to leave. Beltzu's answer to the same phenomenon was that running is wrong.

People, like the Mazuhren themselves, ought to accept the Mazuhrat. Death and all. You can see why Azwighen preferred him elsewhere. Two religions out of one storm, and fourteen centuries on they're still the only declared two on this continent.
Monks And Priests

I've mentioned that Beltzu chose exile over a second drowning. An important caveat to that is that this is the Mazuhren version of events, and also the widely accepted one. The Zwigots think differently.

In one of their better known legends, Beltzu never made an incorrect reading, and was scorned by the Mazuhren for his success, and for gathering a following that contradicted their teachings. So they put him to the drowning meaning to kill him, and he survived it.
They did it again, and again, for a year, before accepting that the man was beyond death and exiling him instead, before he could be taken for a martyr.

It's the same trick every priesthood pulls on its founder's worst day, and I'd have more patience for it if the Mazuhren version didn't have one hundred and sixty-nine names attached. Which leads me to an obvious point. The two religions don't get along. Who would have thought.

Zwigots are banned from entering Lastrago, and I can't tell you when that started. The temple records treat the prohibition as something that was always true, which in my experience means somebody lost an argument nobody wanted written down. Anyway.

A Zwigot found in a Lastragan village is most likely beaten to death, and then hanged regardless. There are more such cases than I care to list. And should one reach Mazuhren hands, as a mockery of their legend, they'll be put to the spire repeatedly until they perish.

What's amusing about the whole thing is that the Zwigots believe this to be a great honor. Retelling the story, becoming one with nature, that sort of thing. Every year some make the journey in hiding, only to reveal themselves to the priests in order to go through the ceremony.
Their brethren will then call them saints. I'd use a different word.
Ashes To Ashes

I'd be surprised if one villager in a thousand could tell you a line from the Tzikhari beyond the ones that have turned into proverbs. It boggles my mind how people just accept the monks on face value: weddings, funerals... Especially funerals. The obvious reason, as always, is practical.

Nobody wants to handle a body that sat outside for three days during summer. And here comes one who would not only do that, but would also only charge you just enough to cover the pyre and a meal or two. But still, the commoners seem so eager to declare one a holy man.

Smear your face with the ashes of the dead, maybe eat some if you're a traditionalist, and there you go - thou art sacred. At least the same can't be said about my peers, thank fuck. Most academics see the Zwigots for what they are. A death cult.

A popular and widely accepted one, but a death cult nonetheless. Their ceremonies are proof enough. While they claim all matter is the same, they seem to revere only the type which disgusts everyone else. They'd claim it is a demonstration of faith, but I see it for what it is.
Showmanship. An attempt to convince the gullible that there is more to them than meets the eye.

A combination of all the above is how they spread. What started as a single temple in Imellah, on the outskirts of Trefgann, spread to the whole region within two generations. The centuries between that and now are harder to trace.
Nobody thought to document a religion that was mostly tolerated and occasionally useful, and by the time anyone noticed it warranted a chapter, the temples were already everywhere. Lastrago excluded.

Governments tolerate their oddities for their free services, and for giving the masses' heads something to play around with which isn't their mandate. The temples are mostly self sufficient: gardening, cooking. It's a simple lifestyle.

They spend most of their time copying books, arguing over the Tzikhari, meditating, and occasionally ceremonial work for the locals. They barely mingle. People are impressed with a monk who's willing to wear their aunt's ashes on their face, but they wouldn't exactly invite him to dinner.

They're still expanding despite that, mostly due to their policy of acceptance. Orphans, Car-Rex, the poor, whoever nobody else wanted. People leave them at the temple door knowing they'll be taken care of for life.

The children learn Old Lastragan before common, in some cases, and are given Lastragan names. They are then expected to recite the Tzikhari by heart. Fail to do so, and you'll be thrown out eventually, which is exactly why most succeed.
The banished are left with no trade, no connections, not even a name.
Modern Lastrago considers the old tongue dead, but the Zwigots speak it freely.

I can't read it myself, which is worth admitting, because it means every Tzikhari translation I've complained about in these pages was made by outsiders working from whatever leaked out of the houses over the centuries.

Which reminds me, Beltzu ends in -u, which is a woman's ending in Old Lastragan. Nobody I've asked has had an explanation, but I do think it's worth pointing out. The monks have argued about this to no end, but in neither of their conclusions is he a woman.
Lost And Found

The Zwigots say Beltzu kept walking west all the way to Knotsreach, and into the Wending, where he is still alive, frozen in meditation, with his tomb built around him. Which, assuming it's real, is what the grand temple of Tzubilek was built around.

Conveniently, nobody outside the order has ever seen the place. It is the seat of the Mukek, "The Caretaker," and reaching it is the doctrine made literal. You walk into the Wending and "Tobol kan, motol ot" - trust the path to deliver you.

When a Mukek dies, the senior houses each send a candidate, and the first to arrive at Tzubilek is declared the next one. A test of faith. To my eyes, the Wending has no opinion on theology, but I don't make the rules, so here we are.
The current Mukek is Chimek, who has been at Tzubilek for some forty years with a handful of monks who made the walk alongside him.
His rulings on the Tzikhari have a reputation I can't personally verify, but the abbots I've pressed on the matter were respectful in a way that suggests he amounts to more than his title.

He settles disputed readings, rules on the correct form for ceremonies, and decides what counts as heresy. He is also dying. I have this from three separate sources in Luznica, though none of them seemed particularly interested in discussing what comes next.
Which brings me to Luznica, where the senior abbot of the local house serves as Ozbekem, "the one who reads on behalf of."

In practice, this means he opens Chimek's correspondence, receives visiting abbots, certifies new houses, and relays the Mukek's rulings whenever they make it out of the Wending. The mundane stuff, in short.

The current Ozbekem is Kanteb, who has held the position for about fifteen years, and who has spent most of those fifteen years answering questions that should be going to Chimek. Not out of ambition. Oh no, he wouldn't dare.

But only because a letter to Tzubilek takes weeks and a ruling takes longer, and the abbot standing in front of Kanteb's desk needs an answer before his village buries someone wrong. So Kanteb answers, carefully, always noting that the Mukek may rule differently.
The Mukek rarely does, partly because Kanteb is cautious enough to stay within safe readings, and partly because for all I know he might as well be dead.

Kanteb doesn't touch political matters, and Chimek can't, and between the two of them the religion has no position on anything outside the Tzikhari. This has suited everyone for fourteen centuries. What concerns me is arithmetic.

The largest religious movement on the continent, present in most villages, handling every birth and death and wedding that matters to ordinary people, and the only thing keeping it out of politics is a dying man in a forest and a cautious abbot who knows better.
Chimek's successor will be chosen by the Wending, and the Wending will produce a scholar.

But the next Ozbekem is just an appointment, and there is nothing in the structure preventing an abbot with ambitions from taking that desk in Luznica and deciding the correspondence is worth answering. Danilo Pescarin was a Remosan nobleman last year. He's an abbot now.
Anyway, when that finally happens, and I'd bet my library that it will in the coming decade, the Zwigots won't be entering politics. They'll be discovering they were already in it.
Rebirth

The Midwives are harder to talk about, mostly because nobody in the houses wants to talk about them. If the world is one substance remaking itself, and the correct response is acceptance, then the question somebody was always going to ask is why stop at acceptance. A rift recycles.
The Green Wall holds back the Mire. One of these, according to the doctrine, is interference. The Midwives want to correct that.

Their literature circulates inside the houses the way these things always do. Copied pages tucked into commentaries, citations disguised as orthodox disputation, arguments that read as hypothetical until you notice they aren't.
I've seen one piece, a six-page tract in translation, and the theology is sound enough that I understood immediately why the Mukek banned it. It doesn't contradict the Tzikhari. It extends it.

The difference between eating a corpse and dismantling the Green Wall, according to the author, is squeamishness, not principle. The mainstream position is that one is acceptance and the other is interference, and the tract asks, politely and at length, where exactly the boundary sits.

The worst incident I'm aware of was in Ezgarin, seventeen eighty-four. Three monks arrested inside the Green Wall buffer zone by an Iron Perimeter patrol. What they were doing there the Remosan report doesn't specify, though the location speaks clearly enough. Two were hanged.

The third, a woman named Idra Chenne, was not recovered. The disavowal from Luznica arrived within the month. One page. Kanteb's predecessor, presumably, though it isn't signed. The Zwigot position, it argues, is that there is no self apart from the substance.

A monk eating a corpse is not doing something to the world. He is the world, consuming itself. The Midwives, the moment they decided the Green Wall should come down, placed themselves outside the process. An agent, acting on the substance, directing it.
Which is the Mazuhren error rebuilt from the other end. The priests flee the storm. The Zwigots withstand it. Tobol kan, motol ot. That's what the page says.
What it doesn't say is that the Zwigots survive on tolerance, and that a religion associated with sabotage and dead Weave agents would not survive very long at all.
The Mukek declared the Midwives heretical, and the houses strip the name from any monk found distributing the literature. This has not, as far as I can tell, done much.
The arguments still circulate, probably because a disputation-based religion has a very hard time telling its monks to stop thinking about something.
Ancient Lastragan
Pronunciation
Tz as in "cats" Ch hard, as in "check" X "sh" (Nabixa = nah-BEE-sha) Stress penultimate
Names
Names are modular: root + ending. Two syllables is common, three is formal. It should sound like a rock hitting another rock.
Vocabulary
Word order: verb first, then subject, then object. Subject drops when obvious from context.
